faq.a: No. It teaches general principles with illustrative numbers. It cannot know your situation, so for decisions about your own money use a qualified professional and official sources.

faq.q: Does it recommend products or shares?
faq.a: No. It explains how different kinds of product work and what to ask, but never says what to buy.
Yes, for examples. The ideas apply in any currency; tax and regulation vary by country.

activities.title: Build a monthly budget
activities.objective: Total income and spending, find what is left and flag overspending.
activities.scenario: Riya earns a monthly stipend and some pocket money. List her spending and see what remains. Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In B3 total the income (B1 and B2).
In B11 total the spending in B5:B10.
In B12 work out what is left (income minus spending).
In B13 show Saving or Overspent with IF.
In C5 work out rent as a percent of income (rent divided by B3); copy the idea for C6.

checks.label: B3 is the total income
checks.explain: Total income is the money coming in each month.

checks.label: B11 is the total spending
checks.explain: Add every spending line.

checks.label: B12 is what is left
checks.explain: Left over is income minus spending.

checks.label: B13 shows Saving
checks.explain: A positive balance means money can be saved.

checks.label: C5 is rent as a share of income
checks.explain: A percentage compares a part with the whole.

checks.label: C6 is food as a share of income
checks.explain: Spending shares show where money goes.

activities.title: How many months could you cope?
activities.objective: Work out an emergency fund target and how long it will take to reach it.
activities.scenario: A family spends 24,000 rupees a month and has saved 30,000. A common target is six months of spending. Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In B4 find how many months of spending the savings cover.
In B5 find the target (months wanted times monthly spending).
In B6 find how much more is needed.
In B7 find how many months it takes to close the gap if they save 3,000 a month (round up with ROUNDUP).

checks.label: B4 is months covered
checks.explain: Savings divided by monthly spending tells how long you could manage.

checks.label: B5 is the target fund
checks.explain: Target is months wanted times monthly spending.

checks.label: B6 is the gap
checks.explain: The gap is the target minus what you have.

checks.label: B7 is the months to close the gap
checks.explain: Divide the gap by what you save each month and round up to whole months.

cells.A7: Months to reach target at 3,000 a month

activities.title: Watch compound interest grow
activities.objective: Build a year-by-year table where each year's interest is added to the balance.
activities.scenario: 10,000 rupees is invested at 8% a year. Compare simple interest (always on the original amount) with compound interest (on the growing balance).
steps: In B6 start the compound balance with the amount in B1; in C6 the simple balance.
In B7 grow the compound balance: previous balance times 1 plus the rate.
In C7 grow the simple balance: the previous balance plus the amount times the rate.
Do the same to row 10 (year 4).
In B12 find how much more compound growth gives than simple after four years.

checks.label: B6 starts at the invested amount
checks.hint: Type =B1 so the balance starts at the amount invested.
checks.explain: Both balances begin with the same amount.

checks.label: B7 is the balance after year 1
checks.explain: Compound growth multiplies the balance by 1 plus the rate.

checks.label: B10 is the compound balance after year 4
checks.hint: Copy the same pattern down to row 10.
checks.explain: After four years: 10,000 times 1.08 to the fourth power.

checks.label: C10 is the simple-interest balance after year 4
checks.explain: Simple interest adds the same amount every year.

checks.label: B12 is the extra from compounding
checks.explain: Interest earned on interest is the extra.

activities.title: Work out a loan's EMI and total cost
activities.objective: Use PMT to find a monthly payment and see how much interest a loan really costs.
activities.scenario: A student takes a laptop loan. Find the monthly instalment, the total repaid and the interest paid for two terms. Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In B5 find the monthly payment for the 12-month loan with PMT (monthly rate = yearly rate / 12; use -B1 so the answer is positive).
In B6 find the total repaid (payment times months).
In B7 find the interest paid (total repaid minus the loan).
Do the same in column C for the 24-month loan.

checks.label: B5 is the 12-month EMI
checks.explain: PMT takes the monthly rate, the number of months and the loan (negative so the result is positive).

checks.label: B6 is the total repaid over 12 months
checks.explain: Total repaid is the payment times the number of months.

checks.label: B7 is the interest paid over 12 months
checks.explain: Interest is what you repay above what you borrowed.

checks.label: C5 is the 24-month EMI
checks.hint: Use C3 for the number of months.
checks.explain: A longer loan has a lower payment.

checks.label: C7 is the interest paid over 24 months
checks.explain: The longer loan costs more in total interest.

activities.title: Real return after inflation
activities.objective: Compare nominal returns with inflation to see whether money really grows.
activities.scenario: Three places to keep 1,00,000 rupees for a year offer different returns. Prices rise by 6% a year. Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In C3:C5 work out the money after one year (amount times 1 plus the return).
In D3:D5 work out the real return: (1 plus nominal) divided by (1 plus inflation) minus 1.
In E3:E5 use IF to show Gains or Loses buying power (real return above zero is a gain).

checks.label: C3 is the money after a year at home
checks.explain: With no return the amount stays the same.

checks.label: C5 is the money after a year in a fixed deposit
checks.explain: A 7% return adds 7,000.

checks.label: D4 is the real return of the savings account
checks.explain: Real return compares growth with price rises.

checks.label: D5 is the real return of the fixed deposit
checks.explain: A 7% return against 6% inflation barely gains.

checks.label: E3 says Loses for cash at home
checks.explain: A negative real return means buying power fell.

checks.label: E5 says Gains for the fixed deposit
checks.explain: A positive real return means buying power rose.

activities.title: Project a monthly saving plan
activities.objective: Use FV to see what regular monthly saving can grow to, and compare it with just saving.
activities.scenario: Dev can save 2,000 rupees a month for 10 years. Compare no growth with an assumed 8% yearly return (an assumption, not a promise). Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In B6 find the total Dev puts in (monthly amount times months).
In B7 find the future value with FV (monthly rate, months, negative payment).
In B8 find the growth (future value minus total put in).
In B9 show what share of the final amount is growth.

checks.label: B6 is the total put in
checks.explain: Total contributions are the monthly amount times the months.

checks.label: B7 is the future value
checks.explain: FV needs the monthly rate, the number of months and the payment (negative).

checks.label: B8 is the growth
checks.explain: Growth is the final amount minus what you put in.

checks.label: B9 is the growth share
checks.explain: A share compares the growth with the final amount.

activities.title: Your net worth statement
activities.objective: Add up what you own and what you owe to find your net worth.
activities.scenario: A young graduate lists assets and debts. Find the net worth and the debt-to-asset ratio. Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In B6 total the assets (B2:B5).
In B12 total the debts (B9:B11).
In B14 work out net worth (assets minus debts).
In B15 work out the debt ratio (debts divided by assets) and in B16 show OK if it is below 0.5, otherwise High.

checks.label: B6 is total assets
checks.explain: Assets are what you own.

checks.label: B12 is total debts
checks.explain: Debts are what you owe.

checks.label: B14 is net worth
checks.explain: Net worth is assets minus debts.

checks.label: B15 is the debt ratio
checks.explain: The debt ratio compares debts with what you own.

checks.label: B16 shows OK
checks.explain: A debt ratio below 0.5 means you own more than twice what you owe.

activities.title: Final project: your first financial plan
activities.objective: Combine a budget, a savings goal, a loan check and a projection in one plan.
activities.scenario: Arun earns 30,000 a month. Build his plan: a budget, a savings rate, a goal, a loan test and a 5-year projection. Educational example only: this is not personal financial advice.
steps: In B3 total the spending lines (B4:B8) and in B9 find what is left.
In B10 find the savings rate (left over divided by income).
In B13 work out the months to reach the 1,80,000 emergency fund target at the monthly saving in B9 (use ROUNDUP).
In B16 find the EMI for the bike loan with PMT (use -B14 as the loan), and in B17 check with IF that the EMI is at most 20% of income: Affordable or Too high.
In B19 project the value of saving B9 each month for 5 years at the assumed return with FV.

checks.label: B3 is total spending
checks.explain: Add every spending line.

checks.label: B9 is the money left
checks.explain: Income minus spending.

checks.label: B10 is the savings rate
checks.explain: A savings rate is the share of income you keep.

checks.label: B13 is the months to reach the target
checks.explain: Target divided by the monthly saving, rounded up.

checks.label: B16 is the EMI
checks.explain: PMT with the monthly rate, the number of months and the loan.

checks.label: B17 says Affordable
checks.explain: A common guide is that loan payments should stay under about a fifth of income.

checks.label: B19 projects the 5-year value
checks.explain: FV with the monthly rate, 60 months and the monthly saving.
